## Objectives

- Explain what an application protocol adds on top of TCP or UDP.
- Find the specification of an Internet protocol, and read the parts
  you need.
- List the decisions a specification has to make.
- Write the specification of a simple text protocol, with sequence
  diagrams.

## What an application protocol is

Your mail program and Google's servers were written by different
people, years apart. They work together because both follow **SMTP**.

An application protocol says:

- which **messages** exist, and what each one means;
- the **format** of each message, down to the bytes;
- the **order**: who speaks first, what may follow what;
- what happens on an **error**.

## On top of TCP and UDP

| Layer | Examples | Takes care of |
|---|---|---|
| Application | SMTP, HTTP, SSH, yours | What the bytes mean |
| Transport | TCP, UDP | Bytes between **programs** |
| Network | IP | Packets between two **machines** |

The transport layer moves bytes. What they mean is up to the
application protocol.

## TCP and UDP

- **TCP**: a reliable, ordered **stream of bytes**. Two messages may
  arrive in one read, one message in several reads.
- **UDP**: independent **datagrams**, each delivered whole, which can be
  lost, duplicated or reordered.
- Everything else is up to the application protocol: up to you, when
  you design one.

## Three families

| Family | Messages are | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Text | Lines of text, JSON | SMTP, POP3, IMAP, HTTP/1.1 |
| On top of HTTP | Requests to resources | Web and mobile APIs (REST) |
| Binary | Fields in bytes | SSH, DNS, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 |

- Text: readable and typeable by a human, easy to debug.
- Binary: compact and fast to parse, needs a tool to read.

## RFCs

- Internet protocols are specified by the **IETF**, in **RFCs**
  (*Request for Comments*).
- Discussed as drafts, then published with a number.
- A published RFC **never changes**: a new version is a new RFC that
  *obsoletes* the old one (IMAP: RFC 3501, then RFC 9051).
- Not every RFC is a standard: each one has a status.
- Status and successors: `datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc3501`.

## Some RFCs

| Protocol | RFC |
|---|---|
| SMTP | 5321 |
| POP3 | 1939 |
| IMAP | 9051 |
| SSH, transport layer | 4253 |
| HTTP semantics | 9110 |
| HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 | 9112, 9113, 9114 |

Long documents (SMTP: 95 pages): read the **examples** first, then the
messages you need. Ports: the **IANA** registry.

## A real exchange: SMTP

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}
```text
S: 220 foo.com Simple Mail Transfer Service Ready
C: EHLO bar.com
S: 250-foo.com greets bar.com
S: 250-8BITMIME
S: 250-SIZE
S: 250-DSN
S: 250 HELP
C: MAIL FROM:<Smith@bar.com>
S: 250 OK
C: RCPT TO:<Jones@foo.com>
S: 250 OK
C: RCPT TO:<Green@foo.com>
S: 550 No such user here
C: RCPT TO:<Brown@foo.com>
S: 250 OK
C: DATA
S: 354 Start mail input; end with <CRLF>.<CRLF>
C: Blah blah blah...
C: ...etc. etc. etc.
C: .
S: 250 OK
C: QUIT
S: 221 foo.com Service closing transmission channel
```
:::

## What it shows

- **Who speaks first**: the server, `220`.
- **Messages**: a keyword and parameters, exact syntax in the RFC.
- **Framing**: lines end with `\r\n`; the text of the mail ends with a
  line holding `.`.
- **Responses**: a three-digit **code** for the program, a text for the
  human. Several lines? `250-` on all but the last.

## What it shows: order, errors, extensions

- **Order**: `MAIL`, then `RCPT`, then `DATA`.
- **Errors**: `550` for Green, Jones and Brown still get the mail.
- **Extensions**: listed in the answer to `EHLO`.
- **End**: `QUIT`, then the server closes the connection.

## The decisions you make

A specification answers each question **explicitly**: every answer left
out becomes a guess in someone else's code.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Transport: TCP or UDP?
- Port?
- Who speaks first, who closes?
- Encoding?
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Framing: where does a message end?
- Format of the messages?
- Errors?
- What about version 2?
:::
::::

## Transport: TCP or UDP

- **TCP**: every message matters, in order (chat, turn-based game, file
  transfer).
- **UDP**: a lost message does no harm, or the application handles
  losses (a sensor, a discovery). Say what happens on a loss.
- You program both in the TCP & UDP chapters. For now: choose, and
  justify.

## Port

The server listens on a port, the client must know it.

| Range | Name | Use |
|---|---|---|
| 0-1023 | System ports | Standard services |
| 1024-49151 | User ports | Assigned to applications by IANA |
| 49152-65535 | Dynamic ports | Never assigned, temporary use |

Your protocol: a port between 1024 and 32767, **unassigned** in the IANA
registry. Above 32768 a Linux client may already hold it.

## Who speaks, which encoding

- The client opens the connection; then either side can **speak first**:
  the server in SMTP, the client in HTTP. Say which.
- Say **who closes**, and when: after `QUIT`, after the answer, when
  the client leaves.
- **Encoding**: write it down. UTF-8.
- A length limit says what it counts: 100 characters in UTF-8 can take
  400 bytes.

## Framing: where a message ends

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
| Framing | How | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Delimiter** | Ends with a chosen character | SMTP (`\r\n`), your PW2 |
| **Length prefix** | Starts with its length | HTTP/1.1 body, binary protocols |
| **Connection close** | Ends when the sender closes | Daytime |
:::

- With a delimiter, the delimiter cannot appear **inside** a message:
  escape it or forbid it.
- With UDP, one datagram is one message, if it fits.

## Message format

One message per line, a **keyword** in capitals, parameters separated
by a space:

::: {.center}
`SEND bob Hello Bob!`
:::

- A parameter that may contain spaces goes **last**: for `SEND`, split
  on the first two spaces, the rest is the text.

## Errors

- For each message, list **every** response, errors included.
- Then the cases tied to no message:
  - an **unknown** message, missing or invalid parameters;
  - a valid message at the **wrong time** (`SEND` before `JOIN`);
  - a client that disappears.
- Give each error a **code** a program can test.

## Extensibility

A protocol lives longer than its first version.

- A new version **adds** messages, and keeps the existing ones as they
  are: same syntax, same meaning.
- An unknown message gets an **error answer**, and the connection stays
  open: a new client can see that an old server does not know a
  command.
- When versions coexist, the first exchange says what each side
  supports, like SMTP's `EHLO`.

## A specification in four sections

1. **Overview**: what for, which problem.
2. **Transport protocol**: TCP or UDP, port, encoding, framing, who
   opens, speaks first and closes, what happens on errors.
3. **Messages**: syntax, parameters, every response with error codes.
4. **Examples**: sequence diagrams, error cases included.

- Section 3: **one action at a time**, request and responses together.
- In Markdown, in your repository.

## Example: the SMS protocol

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
Named users send short messages (at most 100 characters) to each other,
through a server.

- TCP, port 6435, UTF-8, one message per line ending with `\n`.
- `JOIN <name>`: `OK`, or `ERROR 1` if the name is taken.
- `LIST`: `CLIENTS alice bob`.
- `SEND <recipient> <message>`: `OK`, or `ERROR 1` / `ERROR 2`.
- The server delivers: `RECEIVE <sender> <message>`.
- The client leaves by closing the connection.
- `RECEIVE` arrives at any time: act on the keyword, never wait for a
  given answer.
:::

## The SMS protocol

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant C1 as Client 1
    participant S as Server
    participant C2 as Client 2
    C1->>S: JOIN alice
    S-->>C1: OK
    C2->>S: JOIN bob
    S-->>C2: OK
    C1->>S: SEND bob Hello Bob!
    S-->>C1: OK
    S->>C2: RECEIVE alice Hello Bob!
```

## Summary

- An application protocol gives a meaning to the bytes TCP or UDP
  carry.
- Real protocols are specified in RFCs: read the examples first.
- Decide transport, port, encoding, framing, messages, order, errors,
  and say it **explicitly**.
- Four sections: overview, transport, messages, examples.
